title: Chip-Stock Hype Cycles: A Quick Guide to Avoiding the Next Bubble
abstract: Another chip-stock frenzy is brewing, and I'm here to tell you why you'll probably get burned again.
body:
## The Great Chip-Stock Hype Cycle: A User's Manual

I've seen this movie before. The plot is always the same: a new technology promises to change everything, a handful of companies become the anointed ones, and investors lose their minds. Right now, it's all about AI chips. Nvidia is the star, TSMC is the enabler, and every other semiconductor stock is riding the wave. But here's the thing: hype cycles are not investment strategies. They're psychological contagions. And if you're not careful, you'll be the one holding the bag when the music stops.

Let me be clear: I'm not saying AI is a fad. I'm saying that the stock market's reaction to AI is a fad. There's a difference. The technology might be transformative, but that doesn't mean every company with 'AI' in its pitch deck is worth a trillion dollars. Remember the dot-com bubble? The internet was real. Pets.com was not. The same logic applies here. Just because TSMC makes the chips that power AI doesn't mean its stock can't be overvalued. Just because Nvidia has a near-monopoly on AI training chips doesn't mean it will forever. Markets have a way of correcting excesses, and the correction is rarely gentle.

## Why This Time Is Not Different

Every bubble comes with a catchy slogan. In the late 1990s, it was 'the new economy.' In the 2000s, it was 'housing never goes down.' Now, it's 'AI is the new electricity.' I'll admit, that one's pretty good. But slogans don't pay dividends. What pays dividends is earnings, and earnings come from selling products people actually need at prices they can afford. Right now, the AI chip market is driven by a handful of hyperscalers—Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta—who are buying up every GPU they can get their hands on. That's great for Nvidia's top line. But what happens when they've built enough capacity? What happens when the ROI on all that AI infrastructure doesn't materialize? The answer: a bloodbath.

I've been around long enough to remember when Cisco was the most valuable company in the world. It made the routers that powered the internet. Sound familiar? Cisco's stock peaked in 2000 and didn't recover for two decades. The internet didn't go away. But Cisco's valuation was based on the assumption that every human on earth would need a router. They didn't. The same will happen with AI chips. Not every company will need a supercomputer. Not every app will need a large language model. And when the market realizes that, the stocks that flew highest will fall hardest.

## The BoJ Factor and Other Macro Landmines

Now, let's talk about the elephant in the room: the Bank of Japan. For years, the BoJ has kept interest rates ultra-low, which made Japanese yen the funding currency of choice for global carry trades. Investors borrow yen cheaply, invest in higher-yielding assets, and pocket the difference. A lot of that money has flowed into tech stocks, including semiconductors. But the BoJ is slowly tightening. When rates rise, the carry trade unwinds. And when the carry trade unwinds, it doesn't just affect Japan. It sucks liquidity out of global markets. Chip stocks, being high-beta and highly speculative, are the first to get hit. You don't need a degree in economics to see the risk. You just need to pay attention.

And it's not just the BoJ. The Federal Reserve is still wrestling with inflation. Geopolitical tensions are simmering. The U.S. election is coming up. Any of these could trigger a risk-off move. When that happens, investors don't discriminate. They sell everything, but they sell the most speculative stuff first. Guess what's speculative? A stock trading at 50 times sales. A stock that's up 200% in a year. A stock that everyone and their grandmother is talking about. That's the definition of a crowded trade. And crowded trades end badly.

## How to Avoid Getting Burned

So, what's an investor to do? First, stop chasing. If you're buying a stock because it's going up, you're not investing. You're gambling. Second, look at valuations. I don't care how great the story is; if the price is insane, the returns will be too. Third, diversify. Don't put all your money in semis. Don't put all your money in tech. Don't put all your money in anything. Fourth, have a plan. Know when you'll sell. Know what would make you change your mind. And fifth, ignore the noise. The financial media is not your friend. They make money from clicks, not from your returns. When they're screaming about the next big thing, it's usually a sign that the easy money has already been made.

I'm not saying you should avoid chip stocks entirely. Some of them are great companies. TSMC is a fantastic business. Nvidia has a moat. But great companies can be terrible investments at the wrong price. And right now, the prices are wrong. The hype is too high. The expectations are too lofty. The risk is too great. So, do yourself a favor: take a step back. Breathe. And remember that the market is a voting machine in the short run and a weighing machine in the long run. Right now, it's voting for AI chips. But eventually, it will weigh them. And when it does, you don't want to be the one left holding the bag.

## The Bottom Line

Bubbles are not new. They're not going away. And they're not always easy to spot when you're in the middle of one. But the signs are always there: euphoria, leverage, and a story that's too good to be true. The AI chip hype cycle has all three. So, if you're thinking about jumping in, ask yourself: are you investing, or are you gambling? If it's the latter, at least admit it. And if it's the former, do your homework. Because the next bubble is already inflating, and it's got your name on it.
